title: Artificial mixing prevents nuisance blooms of the cyanobacterium Microcystis in Lake Nieuwe Meer, the Netherlands
authors: Visser PM, Ibelings BW, van der Veer B, Koedood J, Mur LR
scale: Whole lake: Lake Nieuwe Meer, Amsterdam (1.32 km², 18 × 10⁶ m³, mean depth 18 m, max 30 m); two compressors (55 kW and 30 kW) feeding seven perforated aeration tubes, 13 m³/min air in total
dose: Deep bubble-plume mixing, continuous April-October 1993; intermittent in spring 1994 and near-continuous July-September 1994
duration: 2 mixed years vs 2 preceding control years
result: Microcystis colonies per litre and per m2 were lower than in the two control years and hardly any scums occurred; community shifted to flagellates, greens and diatoms. Volumetric chlorophyll fell but depth-integrated chlorophyll (per m2) increased; intermittent mixing cut energy costs 75% while still preventing stratification.
env_effects: Stratification removed, homogeneous temperature and oxygen; no oxygen problems reported. Intermittent spring mixing cut energy use by 75% in April-June 1994 (whole-season 1994 energy 27% of 1993). Depth-integrated chlorophyll (per m²) increased with mixing.
key_details: Whole-lake before-after comparison: two mixed years (1993, 1994) against two preceding unmixed control years (1990, 1991), no separate control lake. Microcystis colonies per litre and per m² were lower in mixed years and hardly any nuisance scums occurred, while the community shifted to flagellates, greens and diatoms. Volumetric chlorophyll fell but areal (m⁻²) chlorophyll and peak areal content rose, so total phytoplankton was not reduced, only redistributed and shifted away from cyanobacteria. Colony buoyancy showed Microcystis escaped entrainment at some distance from the plumes. Works because the lake is deep (mixing depth >> euphotic depth).
fulltext_discrepancy: Full text notes total depth-integrated phytoplankton biomass increased under mixing; benefit is a species shift away from Microcystis, not less algae overall.

title: Artificial mixing to reduce growth of the blue-green alga Microcystis in Lake Nieuwe Meer, Amsterdam: an evaluation of 7 years of experience
authors: Jungo E, Visser PM, Stroom J, Mur LR
scale: Lake Nieuwe Meer, 1.3 km2, max depth 30 m, TP 500 mg/m3
dose: Bubble-plume installation, 85 kW installed compressor power, summer operation
result: Microcystis mass up to 20 times lower than before mixing and no scums; shift to flagellates, greens and diatoms. Total phosphorus and nitrogen unchanged; chlorophyll-a lower by dilution but transparency did not improve.
env_effects: Surface ~2 °C cooler; oxygen >5 mg/L throughout, widening fish habitat; 85 kW continuous energy use.

title: Changes in turbulent mixing shift competition for light between phytoplankton species
authors: Huisman J, Sharples J, Stroom JM, Visser PM, Kardinaal WEA, Verspagen JMH, et al.
organism: Microcystis vs diatoms and green algae
scale: Lake Nieuwe Meer, Amsterdam (1.3 km2, mean depth 18 m, max depth 30 m, hypertrophic); 3 sampling stations
dose: Air bubbling from seven perforated air tubes laid just above the sediment (running since 1993); turbulent diffusivity measured with SCAMP microstructure profiler
duration: Mixing switched off 19 July - 7 August 2002 and back on, turbulence measured under both regimes; model simulations
result: Mean turbulent diffusivity was 0.17 cm2/s with mixing off and 5.1 cm2/s with mixing on (t test P < 0.0001); the model puts the Microcystis-vs-diatoms/greens switch at D of about 3.4 cm2/s, so artificial mixing moves the lake into the diatom/green-dominated regime. The observed replacement of Microcystis by diatoms and greens is cited from earlier work (Visser et al. 1996a), not new counts.
env_effects: Community composition shift; mechanism is light competition, not cell damage.
key_details: Huisman et al. 2004 parameterised a light-competition model for Microcystis versus lumped diatoms and greens in Lake Nieuwe Meer. Mixing was switched off for about 3 weeks in July-August 2002: the lake stratified within 10 days (thermocline ~5 m) and phytoplankton concentrated in the top 2.5 m. Diffusivity averaged 0.17 cm2/s (N = 105) off vs 5.1 cm2/s (N = 110) on. The model predicts Microcystis surface blooms above 5 x 10^6 cells/mL under weak mixing and diatom/green dominance under intense mixing, with the boundary at D of about 3.4 cm2/s for 18 m depth. No new Microcystis biomass reduction figure is given; it is a mechanism and model-validation paper.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says 'multi-year lake experiment'; the new field work is a ~3-week mixing switch-off in summer 2002 plus modelling. The species shift itself is taken from earlier Nieuwe Meer studies.

title: Controlling the Growth of Microcystis Using Surged Artificial Aeration
scale: Tegeler See, Berlin (4 km2, max depth 16 m, mean depth 6 m); 15 Limnox hypolimnetic aerators at 12-16 m depth (installed 1980)
dose: Continuous summer aeration (1989, 1990), no aeration (1992), surge aeration events after stable stratification (1993, 1994); mixing tracked with the Lake number
result: Continuous aeration did not affect Microcystis population dynamics in 1989 and 1990, even with Lake numbers below 1, and favoured Microcystis over Ceratium. Surge aeration events in 1993 and 1994 were each followed by a Microcystis decline and delayed its growth, although a stock persisted into September; no percentage reduction is given.
env_effects: Surge aeration had no noticeable effect on the distribution of total inorganic nitrogen or total phosphorus. TP was also falling year on year from external remediation (>50 ug/L in 1989-92 to 30-40 ug/L in 1994), a confounder. Continuous aeration suppressed Ceratium.
key_details: Single-lake, multi-year observational comparison of aerator operating schemes, with no control lake and no replication within years. Evidence is qualitative from time series of Microcystis and Ceratium biomass against Lake number (figure only, no tabulated numbers). Microcystis formed very large colonies (up to tennis-ball size) and adapted to continuous mixing. The author concludes surge aeration after prolonged stability hinders slow-growing Microcystis, while continuous aeration strengthens it against Ceratium. Declining phosphorus over 1993-94 confounds the surge-year comparison.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies a clean 3-scheme test; in fact the aerated years were 1989-90, non-aerated 1992 and surge 1993-94, while TP fell over the same period, so the surge effect is confounded and unquantified.

title: The long-term effect of artificial destratification on phytoplankton species composition in a subtropical reservoir
authors: Antenucci JP, Ghadouani A, Burford MA, Romero JR
scale: North Pine Dam (Lake Samsonvale), Brisbane: volume 2x10^8 m3, surface area 19.7 km2, supplies ~30% of Brisbane's water
dose: Bubble-plume destratifier installed 1995: compressor pumping 200 L/s of air through a 90 mm pipe with 33 hole clusters ~17 m apart; runs mid-September to end of April
duration: Phytoplankton record from 1983 (weekly to 1998, then fortnightly); temperature/DO compared 1978-94 vs 1998-2002; chlorophyll trends 1984-2002
result: After destratification most taxa increased significantly at the dam wall: Cylindrospermopsis rose from 5584 to 9372 cells/mL and Microcystis from 313 to 1829 cells/mL (randomised intervention analysis, P < 0.025). Only the rate of eutrophication slowed: the chlorophyll a increase fell from 0.74 to 0.49 ug/L per year (~30%).
env_effects: Thermocline gradient fell from 1 to 0.2 degC/m; the low-DO (<1 mg/L) period shrank from 7 to 3 months and its vertical extent from 15 to <2 m above the bottom. The destratifier's horizontal influence was limited, and upstream sites stayed more stratified.
key_details: Before-after design at one reservoir with no control reservoir; intervention effects tested by randomised intervention analysis on surface cell counts (sample sizes about 77-507 before and 46-220 after per genus). Significant increases after destratification for cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Cylindrospermopsis, Microcystis, Planktolyngbya, Pseudanabaena), several chlorophytes and diatoms. Chlorophyll a kept rising, but more slowly (0.74 to 0.49 ug/L per year for the full record). Sampling methods changed after 1997, and retention time varies from 1 month to 3 years, which confounds before-after comparisons.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record correctly flags a negative result but gives no numbers; the full text shows the dominant toxic cyanobacteria increased (Cylindrospermopsis +68%, Microcystis ~5.8x in mean cells/mL), so effect_pct should be negative (-68 for Cylindrospermopsis).

title: A comparison of phytoplankton community assemblages in artificially and naturally mixed subtropical water reservoirs
scale: North Pine Reservoir (21.8 km², destratification system since 1995) vs unmixed Somerset (42.1 km²) and Wivenhoe (107.5 km²); 4-5 sites each, fortnightly
dose: Destratification unit operated in wet summer months
result: All three reservoirs stayed cyanobacteria-dominated (same three genera = 75-80% of abundance). Colonial species were lower in the mixed reservoir, but C. raciborskii and Planktolyngbya peaked earlier, and mixing may favour species that store low phosphate such as C. raciborskii.
env_effects: Surface phosphate near detection limit in mixed reservoir; possible selection for Cylindrospermopsis.
key_details: Observational comparison of one artificially destratified reservoir with two adjacent unmixed reservoirs in SE Queensland. Phytoplankton was sampled fortnightly at 4-5 sites per reservoir, 1997-2003; nutrients were sampled monthly at the wall site. There was no treated-reservoir replication and no before-mixing baseline, since mixing began in 1995. Total phytoplankton density did not differ significantly among the three reservoirs (P > 0.05), and all three were cyanobacteria-dominated. Species composition at the wall site differed in North Pine (ANOSIM P < 0.01). Surface phosphate in North Pine sat near the detection limit (0.06 µM) and did not correlate with algal density there.

title: Understanding the role of induced mixing for management of nuisance algal blooms in an urbanized reservoir
scale: Ford Lake, Michigan (reservoir); managed hypolimnetic withdrawal
dose: Selective hypolimnetic discharge through dam flood gates, target ~300,000 m³/d (sized to sediment oxygen demand of 0.67 g O2/m²/d), applied adaptively when DO declined
result: With selective hypolimnetic withdrawal in 2008-2011, maximum gaps between deep-mixing events were 10-18 d, the hypolimnion stayed mostly oxic and no nuisance cyanobacterial blooms occurred; in drought year 2012 (no withdrawal) the lake stayed stratified 35 d, sediments released P, and an Aphanizomenon bloom followed a cold-front mixing event.
env_effects: Hypolimnetic oxygenation; depends on upstream water availability.
key_details: Observational before/after-style field study in Ford Lake, Michigan (17.4 × 10⁶ m³ hydroelectric reservoir), June-August 2008-2012, with YSI temperature (6 depths), DO (3 depths) and one chlorophyll fluorescence sensor at 3 m logged every 30 min, plus weekly P sampling. No separate control lake; 2012 (drought, no withdrawal) serves as an unplanned contrast year, n = 1. Convective cooling, not wind, dominated mixing energy (KEstir < 1 J/m²/h 99.4% of the time). In August 2012 lake TP export exceeded river input by 11.3 µg/L (SE 3.7, n = 5), about 164 kg P for the month. Even 300,000 m³/d did not guarantee deep mixing in 2010-2011 around the solstice. Blooms were tracked by fluorescence and microscopy, not quantified as a % reduction.

title: Controlling Eutrophication via Surface Aerators in Irregular-Shaped Urban Ponds
authors: Hao A, Kobayashi S, Xia D, Mi Q, Yan N, Su M, et al.
scale: Two urban ponds in Wenzhou, China: ZS pond (5 surge aerators, 1.5 kg O2 kW⁻¹ h⁻¹, 500 rpm, installed late 2018) and MA pond (9 aerators, 18 sites)
duration: ZS: one June survey before (2018) vs one after (2019); MA: 10 surveys Mar 2018 - Mar 2019, two years after installation
result: DO rose 1.8 to 8.1 mg/L and TP fell 1.6 to 0.4 mg/L and no cyano-blooms occurred, but Microcystis still dominated and chlorophyll-a rose from 29 to 51 µg/L while transparency fell 81 to 27 cm. Authors conclude aeration can promote algal growth.
env_effects: Better oxygen, less sediment P release; higher chlorophyll and lower clarity.
key_details: Uncontrolled before/after design in ZS pond: a single June 2018 survey vs a single June 2019 survey, with no reference pond. After aeration, DO rose from 1.8 ± 0.4 to 8.1 ± 1.2 mg/L and TP fell from 1.64 to 0.44 mg/L. Chl-a still rose from 29 to 51 µg/L, and Microcystis dominated in both years. MA pond was only surveyed after installation: 10 monthly visits at 18 sites, with DO always >5.7 mg/L, TP 0.03-0.07 mg/L, green algae and diatoms dominant and no blooms. Chl-a was higher on the north side, where aerator coverage differed.

title: Water-lifting aerator reduces algal growth in stratified drinking water reservoir: Novel insights into algal metabolic profiling and engineering applications
authors: Zhang H, Yan M, Huang T, Huang X, Yang S, Li N
organism: Field: mixed reservoir phytoplankton dominated by Bacillariophyta and Chlorophyta (cyanobacteria at most 7.58% relative abundance); lab: Microcystis aeruginosa
scale: Lijiahe drinking-water reservoir (China) plus lab hydrodynamic simulation
dose: Eight water-lifting aerators at full load, ~30 m3/h air each, 24 h/day; lab analogue: 6 or 25 degC, light or dark
duration: Field: operated 29 July - 12 October 2019, sampled 28 July, 25 August and 17 October; lab: 72 h (sampled 0-72 h)
result: Surface algal density fell by more than 90% during aerator operation and kept falling after shutdown, with chlorophyll a and photosynthetic yield (mean Fv/Fm 0.435 to 0.074) also falling. In the lab, M. aeruginosa declined only under 6 degC dark (max drop 1.04 x 10^5 cells/mL, 37.08 ug/L chl a).
env_effects: Lower surface water temperature, more uniform vertical profiles of algae, temperature, pH and DO. The cyanobacteria share rose slightly after operation (max 7.58% at 30 m).
key_details: Field study at Lijiahe Reservoir (Xi'an, China) with one before, one during and one after sampling date at 7 depths (0-bottom), triplicate analyses (n = 3), and no control reservoir or site. The '>90%' surface density decrease is confounded by season (July to October) and by mixing moving cells to depth rather than removing them. The lab arm simulated surface (25 degC light) vs bottom (6 degC dark) conditions for M. aeruginosa; growth stopped and cells, dehydrogenase, ATP and photosynthesis fell under cold dark conditions. The reservoir community was mostly diatoms and green algae, not Microcystis.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record implies a Microcystis bloom was controlled in the field; the field phytoplankton was diatom/green dominated (cyanobacteria <=7.58%) and Microcystis was only a lab culture. The full text gives a >90% surface density reduction (unreplicated, seasonally confounded); lab cultures ran 72 h, not 48 h.

title: Management strategies for a eutrophic water supply reservoir - San Roque, Argentina
authors: Antenucci JP, Alexander R, Romero JR, Imberger J
dose: Bubble-plume diffusers and surface impellers with draft tubes, alone and combined
result: The best simulated design combined a deep and a shallow diffuser: the deep one breaks the seasonal thermocline to limit sediment nutrient release and anoxia, the shallow one deepens surface-layer mixing. No numeric reduction in the abstract.
env_effects: Predicted reduction in anoxia and sediment nutrient release.

title: Artificial destratification options for reservoir management
authors: Chaaya F, Miller BM, Gordos MA, Tamburic B, Felder S
scale: Global review of 138 bubble-plume and mechanical-mixer systems in 114 reservoirs
dose: Air flow per reservoir volume ('volumetric destratification coefficient')
result: Of 59 bubble-plume cases reporting cyanobacteria, 37% reduced them, 12% partly, 34% had no effect and 17% increased them; where thermal destratification succeeded, 63% reported full or partial reduction, and where it failed all 6 cases saw no reduction or an increase. Mechanical mixers: of 12 cases, 5 successful, 2 partial, 3 no improvement, 2 net negative.
env_effects: Successful destratification raised DO and lowered Mn and Fe; cold-water pollution mitigated.
key_details: Global literature review of 138 destratification systems (84% bubble plume, 16% mechanical mixers) in 114 reservoirs, scored against success criteria for thermal, DO, nutrient/metal and cyanobacteria outcomes. Cyanobacteria outcomes were far more variable than thermal or DO outcomes. Reservoirs >100,000 ML had only 30% full/partial success vs 53% in smaller ones; >15 m deep 54% vs 47% for shallower. Cyanobacteria success tracked the volumetric destratification coefficient (air flow per volume); all 5 successful mechanical-mixer cases used draft tubes. Caveat: case reports are heterogeneous and success categories are qualitative, not % biomass change.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says reduction was 'mixed'; full text quantifies it: only 37% of 59 bubble-plume cases fully succeeded and 17% made cyanobacteria worse.

title: A critical review on operation and performance of source water control strategies for cyanobacterial blooms: Part II-mechanical and biological control methods
authors: Kibuye FA, Zamyadi A, Wert EC
scale: Review of artificial mixing, hypolimnetic aeration, dredging, sonication, biological methods in drinking-water sources
result: Optimised mixing and hypolimnetic oxygenation raised DO, cut internal nutrient loading and reduced ions, but benefits were often offset by continued external nutrient inputs and were derailed by organic sedimentation or low Fe/P sediments. Sonication field findings were contradictory.
env_effects: Artificial mixing: resuspension of sediment nutrients/ions, sedimentation of organic matter, warming of the water column may impact cold-water habitats; ineffective in shallow, large-surface-area waters; may need continuous operation.
key_details: Narrative review of mechanical (artificial mixing, hypolimnetic oxygenation/aeration, dredging, sonication) and biological (biomanipulation, macrophytes, barley straw) cyanobacteria controls in drinking-water sources, with tables of field and pilot studies. Artificial mixing is credited with DO increase, suppressed release of P, Fe, Mn and NH3, and cyanobacterial control via light limitation and sedimentation, with benefits up to 7 years under continuous operation; hypolimnetic oxygenation 10-23 years. Main conclusion: all these methods give temporary relief and are commonly derailed by continued external nutrient inputs, so external loading must be controlled first. Sonication lacks field-scale validation. No pooled effect size.
